lead: Cp − Cv is the extra heat a substance needs at constant pressure because it also expands. The difference follows from the equation of state through two PVT derivatives: thermal expansion coefficient α and isothermal compressibility κ_T. The same derivatives give how Cp and Cv change with pressure and volume, and the ratio γ = Cp/Cv. These relations turn table data into heat capacities for liquids and real gases. Only a few universities teach this inside Unit 4.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.3 for Maxwell relations, plus heat capacities from Unit 1 and PVT behaviour from Unit 2.

blocks.text: At constant volume, heat raises internal energy only. At constant pressure, heat also pays for expansion work. So Cp is always larger than Cv. The gap depends on how fast volume grows with temperature and how hard the fluid is to compress.
Let v be molar volume in m³ mol⁻¹, T temperature in K, α thermal expansion coefficient in K⁻¹, and κ_T isothermal compressibility in Pa⁻¹.
Cp − Cv = T v α² / κ_T = −T (∂P/∂T)_V² / (∂P/∂V)_T
blocks.where: Cp and Cv are molar heat capacities in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; α = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)_P; κ_T = −(1/v)(∂v/∂P)_T.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas α = 1/T and κ_T = 1/P. Substitution gives Cp − Cv = R, where R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items: Read T and v from the problem.
Look up α and κ_T in tables.
Compute Tvα²/κ_T in consistent SI units.

blocks.text: For liquids α is small and κ_T is very small, so Cp − Cv is only a few J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, not R.

sections.h3: Ratio and pressure or volume dependence

blocks.text: Define γ = Cp/Cv. For ideal monatomic gas γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67; for ideal diatomic gas γ = 7/5 = 1.40 at ordinary temperature.
Heat capacities are not truly constant. Their slopes come from second derivatives of the equation of state:

blocks.where: v is molar volume; the derivative is at fixed T.
Cv is molar heat capacity at constant volume.

blocks.text: For an ideal gas both second derivatives are zero, so Cp and Cv depend only on T. For a real gas or liquid they drift with pressure or volume. The Gibbs-Helmholtz relation is a cousin: (∂(G/T)/∂T)_P = −H/T², with G Gibbs energy and H enthalpy.
A common use is checking whether tabulated Cp at 1 bar can be used at 50 bar; integrate the pressure derivative.

examples.question: Liquid water at 300 K has v = 18.0 × 10⁻⁶ m³ mol⁻¹, α = 2.57 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, and κ_T = 4.50 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹. Calculate Cp − Cv in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
steps: Write the relation: Cp − Cv = T v α² / κ_T.
Round to three significant figures: 0.793 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
examples.answer: Cp − Cv = 0.793 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for liquid water at 300 K.

traps: Using Cp − Cv = R for a liquid. R applies only to an ideal gas.
Mixing mass volume with molar volume; v must be m³ mol⁻¹.
Getting the sign of α or κ_T wrong; κ_T is defined with a minus sign.
Forgetting to square α, or using T in °C instead of kelvin.
Using v in cm³ mol⁻¹ without converting to m³ mol⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why is Cp greater than Cv for a real gas?
quiz.a: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same temperature rise.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas show Cp − Cv = R using α = 1/T and κ_T = 1/P.
quiz.a: T v (1/T²)/(1/P) = vP/T = R because v = RT/P.

quiz.q: A liquid has α = 0 and finite κ_T. What is Cp − Cv?
quiz.a: Zero, because the formula contains α²; no thermal expansion means no extra expansion work.

quiz.q: If v doubles while α and κ_T stay fixed, what happens to Cp − Cv?
quiz.a: It doubles, because Cp − Cv is proportional to v.

quiz.q: What does (∂Cp/∂P)_T = 0 mean for an ideal gas?
quiz.a: Cp does not change with pressure at fixed T; it depends only on T.

quiz.q: Why is γ = Cp/Cv greater than 1 for a stable phase?
quiz.a: Cp is greater than Cv because constant-pressure heating includes expansion work.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store α and κ_T for each stream and use these relations to convert between Cp and Cv. In cryogenics, the small Cp − Cv of liquids matters for heat-leak estimates. Search “isobaric thermal expansion coefficient database” and “isothermal compressibility of water” for data.
